clause.heading: Defined Terms
clause.text: "Customer Data" means all data, content and materials uploaded to the Service by or on behalf of Customer. "Fees" means the subscription fees set out in the Order Form. "Service" means Provider's hosted note-taking and knowledge management platform. "Term" has the meaning given in Section 4. "Confidential Information" means any non-public information disclosed by one party to the other that is marked confidential or would reasonably be understood to be confidential. "Feedback" means suggestions or comments about the Service provided by Customer.

verdict.rationale: Clause 1.1 is a standard definitions section with no applicable playbook rule (topic 'other' has no rules). Each term is neutral or mutual: "Customer Data" means data uploaded by/on behalf of Customer; "Fees" are the subscription fees in the Order Form; "Service" describes Provider's platform; and "Confidential Information" is defined mutually as information disclosed by one party to the other. The cross-reference for "Term" points to Section 4 (verified: 12-month initial term with auto-renewal), whose substance belongs to clause 4.2 rather than this definitions clause, so it does not make 1.1 one-sided. No never-accept rule applies; acceptable as boilerplate.

clause.heading: Access
clause.text: Subject to this Agreement, Provider grants Customer a non-exclusive, non-transferable right to access and use the Service during the Term for Customer's internal business purposes.

verdict.rationale: Clause 2.1 grants Customer a 'non-exclusive, non-transferable right to access and use the Service during the Term for Customer's internal business purposes.' This is ordinary SaaS license boilerplate: it is limited to the Term, scoped to internal business use, and subject to the rest of the Agreement (which governs fees, data processing, IP, etc.). No playbook rule specifically addresses an access grant, and nothing in the clause is one-sided or unusual. No cross-references were detected that could undermine it.

clause.heading: Service Levels
clause.text: Provider shall use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Service available 99.5% of the time in each calendar month, excluding scheduled maintenance notified at least 48 hours in advance.
clause.section_path: 2 Provision of the Service > 2.2 Service Levels

verdict.rationale: Clause states 'Provider shall use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Service available 99.5% of the time in each calendar month, excluding scheduled maintenance notified at least 48 hours in advance.' This is a standard service-level commitment; the playbook has no rule for service levels (lookup_playbook returned no rules), and the wording is balanced and not one-sided, so it is acceptable as ordinary boilerplate.

clause.heading: Invoicing
clause.text: Fees are invoiced annually in advance and are payable within thirty (30) days of the invoice date.

verdict.rationale: Clause 3.1 provides for annual prepayment with Net 30 terms ('payable within thirty (30) days of the invoice date'), which matches the playbook's primary position under PB-04 ('Net 30 payment terms'). No never_accept items are triggered: no non-refundability, suspension, interest rate, or mid-term price change language appears. Annual prepayment is standard SaaS practice and not contradicted by any rule.

clause.heading: Late Payment and Non-Refundability
clause.text: All Fees are non-refundable under any circumstances, including where Customer terminates this Agreement for Provider's breach. Overdue amounts accrue interest at three percent (3%) per month or the maximum rate permitted by law, whichever is lower, and Provider may suspend the Service without notice if any amount is more than five (5) days overdue.
clause.section_path: 3 Fees and Payment > 3.2 Late Payment and Non-Refundability

verdict.rationale: Clause 3.2 conflicts with playbook rule PB-04 (Payment terms, late fees, refunds) on three points: (1) 'All Fees are non-refundable under any circumstances, including where Customer terminates this Agreement for Provider's breach' matches the never_accept item 'Fees non-refundable even where Provider is in breach'; (2) interest of 3% per month exceeds both the position cap ('at most 1.5% per month') and the never_accept threshold ('Interest above 2% per month'); (3) 'Provider may suspend the Service without notice if any amount is more than five (5) days overdue' conflicts with the position requiring suspension only after 30 days overdue and written notice, and matches the never_accept item 'Suspension without notice'. A redline was proposed using PB-04's preferred_language: Net 30 payment terms, interest per the Swedish Interest Act, suspension only after 30 days of unpaid undisputed amount following written notice, and pro rata refund of prepaid Fees if Customer terminates for Provider's material breach.
verdict.anchor_text: All Fees are non-refundable under any circumstances, including where Customer terminates this Agreement for Provider's breach. clause.heading: Price Changes
clause.text: Provider may increase the Fees at any time by posting revised pricing on its website, and such increase shall apply to the current Term.

verdict.rationale: Clause states: "Provider may increase the Fees at any time by posting revised pricing on its website, and such increase shall apply to the current Term." This conflicts with playbook rule PB-04 (payment), whose position is "No price changes during a committed term" and whose never_accept list includes "Price changes taking effect during the current term." The clause also lacks any written notice requirement or cap on the increase. A redline has been proposed aligning with the fallback position: fees fixed for each Term, increases of at most 5% per year permitted only upon renewal, with at least 60 days' prior written notice.
verdict.anchor_text: Provider may increase the Fees at any time by posting revised pricing on its website, and such increase shall apply to the current Term.

Playbook rule PB-05 (ip_ownership) governs ownership of Customer Data and Feedback only; this clause concerns Provider's own Service IP and does not touch Customer Data or Feedback, so it is ordinary SaaS boilerplate. No cross-references detected. Marked for human review to confirm that "improvements thereto" should be read as improvements to the Service (not to Customer Data).

clause.heading: Customer Data and Feedback
clause.text: Customer retains ownership of Customer Data. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Customer hereby assigns to Provider all rights, title and interest in any Feedback and in any derivative works, analyses and aggregated datasets created from Customer Data, and Provider may use such derivative works for any purpose without restriction.
clause.section_path: 5 Intellectual Property > 5.2 Customer Data and Feedback

verdict.rationale: Clause 5.2 states: 'Customer hereby assigns to Provider all rights, title and interest in any Feedback and in any derivative works, analyses and aggregated datasets created from Customer Data, and Provider may use such derivative works for any purpose without restriction.' This conflicts with playbook rule PB-05 (ip_ownership), which requires that Customer owns everything derived from Customer Data including aggregated datasets, that Provider receives only a licence to host/process the data for the Service, and that Feedback be licensed non-exclusively but never assigned. The clause's assignment of derivative works and 'any purpose without restriction' language fall within PB-05's never_accept list.

clause.heading: Exceptions
clause.text: Confidential Information does not include information that is or becomes publicly available through no fault of the receiving party, was known to the receiving party before disclosure, or is independently developed without use of the disclosing party's information. A party may disclose Confidential Information where required by law or court order, provided it gives the other party prompt notice where legally permitted.

verdict.rationale: Clause 6.3 enumerates the standard exceptions: 'information that is or becomes publicly available through no fault of the receiving party, was known to the receiving party before disclosure, or is independently developed without use of the disclosing party's information,' plus a legally-required-disclosure carve-out with prompt notice ('A party may disclose Confidential Information where required by law or court order, provided it gives the other party prompt notice where legally permitted'). These match PB-06's stated position that 'Standard exceptions (public, already known, independently developed, legally required disclosure)' are acceptable. The clause is mutual in form and no never_accept items apply.

clause.heading: Cap on Liability
clause.text: Subject to Section 12, each party's aggregate liability arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall not exceed the total Fees paid or payable by Customer in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to the claim.
clause.section_path: 8 Limitation of Liability > 8.1 Cap on Liability

verdict.rationale: Clause 8.1 on its face matches PB-01: 'each party's aggregate liability ... shall not exceed the total Fees paid or payable by Customer in the twelve (12) months preceding the event giving rise to the claim' — a mutual cap at 100% of trailing 12-month fees, which is the playbook position. However, the clause opens with 'Subject to Section 12,' and Section 12 states: 'The limitations in Section 8 shall not apply to Customer's payment obligations, Customer's indemnification obligations under Section 9.1, or any breach by Customer of Section 2 or Section 6. For the avoidance of doubt, the limitations in Section 8 shall continue to apply to all liabilities of Provider, including Provider's indemnification obligations under Section 9.2.' This asymmetric carve-out removes the cap for Customer's payment, indemnity, and ordinary breaches (Sections 2 and 6) while expressly preserving it for all of Provider's liabilities — matching PB-01's never_accept item: 'Carve-outs that remove the cap for the Customer's indemnity or ordinary breach while keeping it for the Provider.' Flagged because the fix likely belongs in Section 12 (or jointly across both clauses), so a human should review them together before deciding on redline wording.

clause.section_path: 8 Limitation of Liability > 8.2 Exclusion of Indirect Damages

verdict.rationale: Clause 8.2 provides: 'Neither party shall be liable for any indirect, incidental, special or consequential damages, or for loss of profits, revenue or data, however arising.' The exclusion is mutual (applies to both parties), which is consistent with PB-01's requirement that the liability framework be mutual and not one-sided. It is standard SaaS boilerplate; no never_accept rule under PB-01 applies, and there are no cross-references that could undermine it. No concrete fix is needed.

clause.heading: Indemnity by Provider
clause.text: Provider shall defend Customer against any third-party claim alleging that the Service infringes a patent, copyright or trademark, provided that Customer promptly notifies Provider of the claim and gives Provider sole control of the defence.

verdict.rationale: Clause 9.2 states: 'Provider shall defend Customer against any third-party claim alleging that the Service infringes a patent, copyright or trademark, provided that Customer promptly notifies Provider of the claim and gives Provider sole control of the defence.' Under PB-08 (never_accept), the Provider IP indemnity must not be conditioned on Provider having 'sole control' with no Customer participation right. Here, giving Provider 'sole control of the defence' is a condition precedent to the indemnity, leaving Customer without any participation right — a direct conflict. Additionally, the clause only obliges Provider to 'defend' rather than 'defend and indemnify', which narrows the scope below PB-08's preferred language.

clause.text: Customer Data may be stored and processed in any country in which Provider or its subprocessors maintain facilities, including the United States, and Provider shall not be required to notify Customer of any change of location.

verdict.rationale: Clause states that 'Customer Data may be stored and processed in any country in which Provider or its subprocessors maintain facilities, including the United States, and Provider shall not be required to notify Customer of any change of location.' This conflicts with rule PB-03 on three never-accept items: (1) processing in 'any country' at Provider's discretion; (2) no obligation to notify subprocessor or location changes; and (3) no reference to a data processing agreement. The proposed redline aligns the clause with the playbook position: EEA storage/processing as default, transfers outside only with prior written consent and an SCC-based DPA, and 30 days' notice of any new subprocessor or location change during which Customer may object.

clause.heading: Security
clause.text: Provider shall maintain administrative, physical and technical safeguards designed to protect the security of Customer Data.

verdict.rationale: Clause 10.2 states: "Provider shall maintain administrative, physical and technical safeguards designed to protect the security of Customer Data." clause.heading: Termination by Provider
clause.text: Provider may terminate this Agreement or suspend the Service at any time for convenience upon ten (10) days' written notice to Customer.

verdict.rationale: Clause 11.1 states: 'Provider may terminate this Agreement or suspend the Service at any time for convenience upon ten (10) days' written notice to Customer.' This grants only Provider a unilateral right to terminate or suspend on just 10 days' notice, which conflicts with playbook rule PB-07 requiring either mutual termination rights of at least 60 days' notice, or a fallback of at least 90 days' notice with a pro rata refund. The clause also allows suspension without specifying any conditions or cure period.

clause.heading: Termination by Customer
clause.text: Customer may terminate this Agreement only at the end of the then-current Term in accordance with Section 4.2.

verdict.rationale: Clause 11.2 states: 'Customer may terminate this Agreement only at the end of the then-current Term in accordance with Section 4.2.' Cross-referenced clause 4.2 requires written non-renewal notice at least 90 days before the end of a 24-month auto-renewing term, so Customer has no mid-term convenience or material-breach termination right and is locked in for up to two years. This conflicts with playbook rule PB-07 (severity high), which requires either both parties may terminate for convenience with equal notice of at least 60 days (with pro rata refund of prepaid Fees) plus a material-breach termination after a 30-day cure period, and lists 'Provider may terminate for convenience on short notice while Customer is locked in for the term' as never_accept. Proposed redline adds (a) convenience termination on 60 days' written notice with pro rata refund of prepaid Fees and (b) material-breach termination after a 30-day cure period, using PB-07's preferred language.

clause.heading: Exclusions from Limitation of Liability
clause.text: The limitations in Section 8 shall not apply to Customer's payment obligations, Customer's indemnification obligations under Section 9.1, or any breach by Customer of Section 2 or Section 6. For the avoidance of doubt, the limitations in Section 8 shall continue to apply to all liabilities of Provider, including Provider's indemnification obligations under Section 9.2.

verdict.rationale: Clause 12 states: 'The limitations in Section 8 shall not apply to Customer's payment obligations, Customer's indemnification obligations under Section 9.1, or any breach by Customer of Section 2 or Section 6. clause.heading: Modifications to this Agreement
clause.text: Provider may modify this Agreement at any time by posting a revised version on its website. Continued use of the Service after posting constitutes acceptance of the revised Agreement.

verdict.rationale: Clause 13 states: 'Provider may modify this Agreement at any time by posting a revised version on its website. Continued use of the Service after posting constitutes acceptance of the revised Agreement.' This conflicts with playbook rule PB-09, which requires that amendments be made only in writing signed by both parties. Two never_accept items are triggered: (1) 'Changes by posting on a website' and (2) 'Changes effective on continued use.' A redline has been proposed using the playbook's preferred language to require mutual written signature for amendments and to limit documentation updates to 30 days' notice without material degradation of the Service or Customer's rights.

clause.heading: Governing Law and Disputes
clause.text: This Agreement is governed by the laws of Sweden. Any dispute shall be finally settled by the courts of Stockholm, Sweden.

verdict.rationale: Clause 14 states 'This Agreement is governed by the laws of Sweden. Any dispute shall be finally settled by the courts of Stockholm, Sweden.' This matches rule PB-10's stated position (Swedish law with the courts of Stockholm) and mirrors its preferred_language verbatim. No never_accept conditions apply: there is no mandatory arbitration outside the EU/EEA and no waiver of mandatory consumer or data-protection rights. No cross-references exist to check.

clause.heading: Assignment
clause.text: Neither party may assign this Agreement without the prior written consent of the other party, not to be unreasonably withheld, except to an affiliate or successor in connection with a merger or sale of substantially all of its assets.

verdict.rationale: Clause 15.1 provides: 'Neither party may assign this Agreement without the prior written consent of the other party, not to be unreasonably withheld, except to an affiliate or successor in connection with a merger or sale of substantially all of its assets.' This is standard mutual boilerplate. Assignment is restricted symmetrically for both parties, consent must not be unreasonably withheld (a reasonableness qualifier that protects the Customer), and the carve-out for affiliates/successors applies equally to both sides. No playbook rule governs assignment, and nothing in the clause is one-sided or unusual.

clause.heading: Entire Agreement
clause.text: This Agreement, together with the Order Form, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior agreements relating to its subject matter.

verdict.rationale: Clause 15.2 provides that 'This Agreement, together with the Order Form, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties and supersedes all prior agreements relating to its subject matter.' This is a standard mutual merger/integration clause: it applies equally to both parties ('between the parties') and appropriately includes the Order Form. No playbook rule governs this topic (topic 'other' has no rules), and nothing in the text is one-sided or unusual, so it falls within ordinary acceptable boilerplate.
